extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, advanced graduate students, and readers interested in mathematical culture, aesthetics, and the theory-vs-problem-solving distinction
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and aesthetic standards for assessing mathematical work and fields, particularly the distinction between 'theory-builders' and 'problem-solvers' and what counts as important, beautiful, or useful mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / self-containedness
rubrics_metrics.description: “One of the attractions of problem-solving subjects, which Gowers collects under the loose mantle ‘combinatorics’, is the easy accessibility of the problems... most papers in combinatorics are self-contained, or demand at most a small amount of background knowledge on the part of the reader. Contrast that with a theorem in algebraic number theory, which might take years to understand if one begins with the knowledge of a typical undergraduate syllabus.” (p. 12)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing work that is readable and usable with modest prerequisite knowledge; an accessibility virtue for problem-solving/combinatorics. Anti-pattern: results or papers that require years of specialized background to even parse, making them inaccessible to most readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connections to other fields (transferability of apparatus)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Two types of appeal which are commonly made to warrant the importance of one’s field are its connections to other fields and its applicability... if one is trying to maximize the size of some structure under certain constraints... choosing an example randomly is likely to give a good answer.” (p.6, p.13 and other passages about applications)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importance may be judged by how a field's concepts, theorems, or tools transfer to other areas (e.g., combinatorics → probability, set theory, cryptography, harmonic analysis, number theory). Examples: the Green–Tao theorem as a cross-field illustration. Anti-pattern: connections that practitioners in another subfield consider the 'wrong sort' and thus unpersuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability / practical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Two types of appeal... are its connections to other fields and its applicability. As for connections with other subjects, there are applications of combinatorics to probability, set theory, cryptography, communication theory... the list goes on and on.” (p. 13)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work gains evaluative value if it yields applications (to other mathematical fields or to real-world problems). Note caveat: the same applications may be judged irrelevant by specialists in another subfield (e.g., a differential geometer may regard some combinatorial applications as not impressive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality versus puzzle/problem value
rubrics_metrics.description: “Now, personally, I think Fermat’s Last Theorem is a ridiculous thing... Rather, it was the activity behind the scenes leading to the proof of the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture that is generally regarded as the major achievement. So, even were results about the existence of arithmetic progressions amongst the primes to be judged similarly as ‘ridiculous’, there might again be some general result lurking behind the scenes.” (TWF 217 quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a result advances general theory or is mainly a stand-alone puzzle. Theory-builders tend to value general structural results and the development of apparatus; problem-solvers may value striking individual problems and techniques. Both kinds of value are legitimate; sometimes a problem's value is in the machinery developed around it rather than the statement alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad guiding principles (e.g., randomness in extremal combinatorics)
rubrics_metrics.description: “if one is trying to maximize the size of some structure under certain constraints, and if the constraints seem to force the extremal examples to be spread about in a uniform sort of way, then choosing an example randomly is likely to give a good answer.” (p. 6)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess work by whether it identifies or exploits high-level principles (heuristics or paradigms) that explain families of phenomena. Example: probabilistic/random construction methods in combinatorics. Guidance: such principles can unify many special cases and serve as a criterion of significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closeness-in-spirit and transferability of mathematicians' skill
rubrics_metrics.description: “Area A is sufficiently close in spirit to area B, that anybody who is good at area A is likely to be good at area B. Moreover, many mathematicians make contributions to both areas.” (p. 14)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge fields by whether expertise and methods translate between them; fields that are 'close in spirit' facilitate cross-pollination and are evidence of deeper unity. This also supports valuing work that bridges such areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-building as powerful organizing framework
rubrics_metrics.description: “Part of the justification for theory building is that it’s the equivalent of building an army tank division rather than using a popular uprising: by optimally structuring things you can accomplish exactly the same things but much, much easier. A good example of this is the theory of generating functions and precise asymptotic estimation of coefficients.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess theories by their ability to systematize, simplify, and make many problems tractable (the 'tank division' metaphor). Examples: generating function theory, Joyal’s species, categorification approaches. Anti-pattern: theories that merely rename or 'get the names right' without delivering computational or explanatory leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository quality: narrative, motivation, and emotional texture
rubrics_metrics.description: “I think Terrence Tao’s informal essays on his formal solutions is the narrative. He provides emotional texture to the subproblems. Numbers ‘want to be primes’ but are prevented by ‘conspiracies.’ This, to me, suggests that this particular genius has learned a method to use both left-brain and right-brain methodologies in optimum combination.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mathematical writing and exposition for clarity, motivating narrative, and intuition. Good exposition can make work more persuasive and accessible; it may reveal purpose and help readers grasp significance. Anti-pattern: dry, opaque presentation that hides motivation and reduces accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor and formal definitions vs pragmatic technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of Joyal’s species versus Wilf’s Generatingfunctionology and comments like: 'Joyal’s definition... discloses a vast horizon of new combinatorial constructions... The simplest, and the most remarkable application... is the rigorous combinatorial rendering of functional composition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between valuing precise, unifying definitions (which can open new directions) and valuing practical, computational techniques that 'pulverise' problems. Both are productive: rigorous frameworks can reveal deeper structure; pragmatic techniques can yield immediate problem-solving power. Anti-pattern: excessive formalism with no evident payoff, or handwaving definitions without rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/long-term impact on the field
rubrics_metrics.description: “The problem-solving of the nineteenth century led to the theory-building of the twentieth.” (Ira Gessel) and other remarks that problem-solving can seed later theory-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work not just for immediate novelty but for its potential to influence future developments (e.g., to motivate new theories). Some work that looks narrow now may catalyze major theoretical advances later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging dialogue and cross-cultural exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: “Gowers ends his essay by encouraging dialogue. Perhaps blogs are the right arenas in which such dialogue might take place.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value venues and work that foster communication between different subcultures (theory-builders and problem-solvers). Practical guidance: use blogs, conferences, and interdisciplinary writing to bridge gaps and surface shared principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness and motivation behind theory development
rubrics_metrics.description: “Developing a theory cannot strictly happen ‘without a specific purpose’ if developed by a human being... Clarification requires some distinction between conscious and unconscious purpose... A mathematician ‘just playing around’ in some domain... is operating... within a paradigm.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether work is driven by clear motivations (conscious or paradigm-driven). Understanding the aims—explanatory, computational, conceptual—helps evaluate significance. Anti-pattern: presenting theory as aimless novelty without situating its goals or expected payoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revealing hidden connections through categorification/abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple posts discuss categorification, species, and 'The Tale of Groupoidification' as a way to 'replace natural numbers by finite sets' and expose links between combinatorics and linear algebra/quantum groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value abstraction/ categorification when it uncovers unexpected relationships between disparate areas (e.g., combinatorics and quantum algebra) and suggests new techniques. Guidance: look for concrete payoffs (new theorems, unified proofs) rather than abstraction for its own sake.
